name: The Troubleshooter's Gauntlet
description: Network troubleshooting — methodology, tools, commands, wireless, and service issues.

nodes.name: The Methodology
nodes.description: CompTIA's 7-step troubleshooting process, OSI layer approaches, and problem documentation.

encounters.title: The Mechanic's Two Approaches: Compare to Spec, or Swap the Part
encounters.scenario: A mechanic diagnosing 'this car feels sluggish' has two complementary approaches. First: compare to BASELINE/SPEC — pull last year's dyno results from when it ran fine and compare to today's readings. If fuel pressure was 50 PSI then and 30 PSI now, that deviation points straight at the fault. Second: COMPONENT SWAP (substitution) — if there's no baseline, swap a suspect part (the fuel pump) for a known-good spare; if the symptom disappears, that part was faulty. In networking, a BASELINE is recorded normal-operation data (bandwidth, latency, error rates) used to spot anomalies. SUBSTITUTION means physically swapping a suspect cable, NIC, port, or transceiver with a known-good one — especially useful when no baseline exists.
encounters.question: A user reports their connection 'feels slow' today. The helpdesk pulls up last month's recorded interface stats for that port (typical: 20% utilization, <5ms latency) and compares them to today's readings (95% utilization, 80ms latency) — immediately pointing to congestion. Separately, a technician with no historical data simply swaps the user's patch cable for a known-good one to see if performance improves. How do these two techniques differ?
options: They're identical — comparing to a baseline IS the same thing as swapping a component

The helpdesk used baseline comparison (current metrics vs recorded normal-operation metrics to spot a deviation); the technician used component substitution (replacing a suspect part with a known-good one to test if the symptom is hardware-related) — most useful when no baseline exists
Baseline comparison only works on wireless networks, while component swapping only works on wired networks
Component swapping should always be tried BEFORE establishing a theory of probable cause, per CompTIA's 7-step process
encounters.explanation: Comparing current metrics to a recorded baseline is data-driven anomaly detection — it shows what changed and by how much. Component substitution is a hypothesis test — swap a suspect part to see if the symptom follows it. They're complementary, not identical; substitution especially shines when no baseline exists. Wrong: (A) one compares numbers, the other tests a physical hypothesis — not the same thing. (C) nothing limits baseline comparison to wireless or substitution to wired — both apply broadly. (D) per the 7-step process, you form a theory (step 2) BEFORE testing it (step 3); randomly swapping parts first is the 'shotgun' anti-pattern.

encounters.title: The Smoke Detector and the New Toaster
encounters.scenario: Imagine a smoke detector starts going off every morning at 7am, starting the exact week someone got a new toaster. You don't need to inspect every wire — the TIMING correlation between 'new toaster' and 'alarm started' is the strongest clue. In networking, when a symptom appears SUDDENLY rather than gradually, the first question should be 'what changed recently?' — a firmware update, ACL edit, new device, config push, or cert rotation. Checking the change management log (RFC history) for anything touching the affected system is often far faster than re-running every diagnostic, because it directly tests the most probable cause of a sudden, isolated symptom.
encounters.question: At 9 AM, multiple finance department users suddenly start getting 'certificate not trusted' warnings on an internal HR portal that worked fine yesterday. No other internal site is affected. Before running any packet captures, what should the technician check FIRST?
options: Immediately replace the HR server's network cable — hardware degrades randomly, so a cable swap is always the right first step

Check the change management log for any changes to the HR portal's certificate, the internal CA, or related infrastructure overnight — a sudden, isolated symptom strongly suggests a recent change is the cause
Re-image every finance department workstation, since a cert error affecting multiple users at once must mean malware
Escalate immediately to the ISP, since certificate errors are always caused by upstream DNS issues
encounters.explanation: A sudden symptom hitting MULTIPLE users at once, isolated to ONE app, is the classic signature of a recent change rather than gradual decay, malware, or a random fault — checking the change log directly tests the most probable cause first. Wrong: (A) cable issues typically affect one user, not many users on one app simultaneously, and swapping hardware first is the 'shotgun' anti-pattern. (C) re-imaging is drastic with no malware evidence, and malware producing an identical cert error across many machines on one site would be unusual versus a simple changed certificate. (D) cert trust errors are a PKI issue, not DNS — escalating to the ISP skips internal investigation.

encounters.question: What is the FIRST step in CompTIA's network troubleshooting methodology?
options: Test a theory
Establish a plan of action
Identify the problem
Document the findings
encounters.explanation: Step 1 is to identify the problem — gather information from users, identify symptoms, reproduce the issue, check recent changes, and review logs. You must understand the problem before theorising about the cause.

encounters.question: After implementing a fix, what is the NEXT step in CompTIA's troubleshooting methodology?
options: Document the findings
Identify the problem again
Verify full system functionality and no side effects
Escalate to the next tier
encounters.explanation: Step 6 is to verify full system functionality after implementing the solution. Check that the original problem is resolved AND that the fix didn't break anything else. Only then proceed to Step 7 (documentation).

encounters.question: Documentation (Step 7 in troubleshooting) is important because:
options: It is only required for compliance reasons
It creates a knowledge base for future troubleshooting and records what changed in the environment
It satisfies the change management requirement for the CAB
It is only done when escalating
encounters.explanation: Documentation records the problem, root cause, steps taken, and resolution — creating institutional knowledge. Future engineers (or your future self) can resolve similar issues faster. It also tracks all changes made to the environment.

encounters.question: The 'divide and conquer' troubleshooting approach typically starts at which OSI layer?
options: Layer 1 (Physical)
Layer 7 (Application)
Layer 3 (Network) — test IP connectivity first to split the problem
Layer 2 (Data Link)
encounters.explanation: Divide and conquer starts at Layer 3 — can you ping the gateway? If yes, the issue is above Layer 3. If no, focus below. This quickly narrows the problem scope without testing every layer sequentially.

encounters.question: A user reports their internet is not working. The FIRST question you should ask is:
options: What browser are you using?
What has changed recently on your computer or network?
Have you tried restarting your computer?
What is your IP address?
encounters.explanation: The most valuable first question in troubleshooting: 'What changed?' Most problems follow a change — a software update, a new cable, a configuration edit, a new device. Identifying the change often leads directly to the root cause.

encounters.question: You test your theory at Step 3 and the fix doesn't resolve the issue. What should you do?
options: Proceed to Step 4 and implement a different fix anyway
Return to Step 2 and establish a new theory of probable cause
Escalate immediately to Tier 2
Skip to Step 7 and document the failure
encounters.explanation: If your theory is proven wrong, go back to Step 2 — establish a new theory. Never implement a fix based on a disproven theory. The methodology is iterative: 1→2→3, if wrong: 2→3, until theory is confirmed, then 4→5→6→7.

encounters.question: Bottom-up troubleshooting starts at Layer 1. What is the correct order?
options: Application → Presentation → Session → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical
Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application
Network → Physical → Application → Transport
Transport → Network → Physical → Application
encounters.explanation: Bottom-up follows the OSI model from Physical (Layer 1) up to Application (Layer 7): Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application. Fix the lowest layer issue first — upper layers often fix themselves.

encounters.question: When should a technician ESCALATE a problem rather than implement a fix?
options: After documenting the issue
When the fix is beyond their skill level, access rights, or authority to implement
After the first failed theory
Only when the problem affects more than 10 users
encounters.explanation: Escalation happens at Step 5 when: the technician lacks the technical skill, doesn't have the required system access, or is not authorised to make the change (e.g., needs CAB approval for a production firewall change). Escalation is not failure — it's the right process.

encounters.question: A user can ping their default gateway but cannot reach internet sites by IP address. Which OSI layer has the problem?
options: Layer 1 or 2 — physical/link issue
Layer 3 — routing issue between the LAN and the internet
Layer 7 — application issue
Layer 4 — TCP port blocked
encounters.explanation: Pinging the gateway confirms Layer 1, 2, and local Layer 3 work. Failing to reach internet IPs (not just names) = routing problem — traffic isn't being forwarded correctly beyond the local gateway. Check the router's default route and upstream connectivity.

encounters.question: A user can ping internet IPs but cannot browse websites by name. Which layer/service has the problem?
options: Layer 1 — physical cable disconnected
Layer 3 — IP routing broken
DNS — name resolution failure (Layer 7 / service)
Layer 4 — TCP handshake failing
encounters.explanation: If ping by IP works but ping/browse by hostname fails — DNS is the problem. IP routing works fine (Layer 3 up to 7 is functional for IP). The host cannot resolve hostnames to IPs. Use nslookup to diagnose DNS.

encounters.question: A switch port shows 'line protocol down' but 'line up'. What does this indicate?
options: Layer 1 physical connection is fine, but Layer 2 is failing (possibly duplex mismatch or keepalive issue)
Physical cable is disconnected
The VLAN is misconfigured
The spanning tree has blocked this port
encounters.explanation: 'Line up' = physical signal detected (Layer 1 OK). 'Protocol down' = Layer 2 failing — keepalive packets not received, duplex mismatch, encapsulation mismatch, or the remote end has a shutdown. This is a classic Cisco IOS show interface output pattern.

encounters.question: You're troubleshooting a connectivity issue. Ping to local hosts works. Ping to gateway fails. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: DNS server is down
IP address, subnet mask, or default gateway misconfiguration on the host
The ISP link is down
A firewall is blocking ICMP
encounters.explanation: Ping to local hosts works = Layer 1/2 and local Layer 3 are functional. Ping to gateway fails = the host likely has the wrong gateway IP, wrong subnet mask (placing gateway in different subnet), or the gateway IP is not configured. Check ipconfig /all.

nodes.name: The Cable Lab
nodes.description: Physical layer faults, cable types, connectors, and troubleshooting tools.

encounters.title: The Right Key for the Right Lock: Fiber Modes and Wavelengths
encounters.scenario: Multimode fiber (MMF) is a wide hallway where light bounces at many angles ('modes') — cheap LEDs/VCSELs at 850nm work fine over short distances (up to ~550m on OM3/OM4 for 10GbE), but those bouncing paths spread out and limit distance. Single-mode fiber (SMF) is a narrow hallway where light travels essentially one straight path — needs a precise laser, usually 1310nm or 1550nm, but can run for tens of kilometers. Key point: an SFP/transceiver is built for a SPECIFIC wavelength and fiber type. Plug an 850nm multimode transceiver into single-mode fiber (or vice versa), and a basic light-source/power-meter test might still detect SOME light at the far end — but the link won't establish, because the receiver can't decode a signal from a mismatched source.
encounters.question: A technician runs a fiber light source and power meter test on a new single-mode run between two buildings — light is detected at the far end within the expected loss budget, so the fiber itself seems fine. But when matching switches are connected via SFPs, the link light never comes up. They discover one SFP is an 850nm multimode transceiver and the other is a 1310nm single-mode transceiver. What's the issue, and why didn't the power meter test catch it?
options: The fiber run is simply too long for any transceiver — distance is the only issue

The two transceivers operate at different wavelengths/fiber types (850nm MMF vs 1310nm SMF) and can't link with each other regardless of fiber condition; a power meter test only confirms the fiber can carry SOME light, not that two specific transceivers are compatible with each other or the fiber type
Power meters can only test copper cabling, so the result is meaningless here
The transceivers must be DAC cables, not SFPs, which is why they're incompatible
encounters.explanation: A power/light test verifies the fiber's physical continuity and loss budget — it says nothing about whether the electronics on each end speak the same 'language.' An 850nm multimode SFP and a 1310nm single-mode SFP use different light sources and wavelengths — they won't link no matter how clean the fiber is. Wrong: (A) nothing indicates the run exceeds single-mode's distance limits — the failure is a transceiver mismatch, not distance. (C) optical power meters are a fiber-only tool, irrelevant to copper. (D) DAC cables are a different medium entirely; the issue is purely SFP wavelength/type mismatch.

encounters.title: The Bundle of Chargers in a Sealed Box
encounters.scenario: Picture a thick bundle of phone chargers, all plugged in and zip-tied together inside a small enclosed box. Each charger gives off a little heat alone — harmless. But bundle hundreds together with no airflow, and the heat compounds, climbing well above room temperature. Copper Ethernet cables carrying PoE work the same way — each cable's conductors warm slightly from the DC current powering devices. In one cable this is negligible. But in a LARGE BUNDLE (50, 100+ cables) carrying high-wattage PoE+ (802.3bt, up to ~90W/port), cumulative heat raises the bundle's internal temperature — and heat increases copper resistance, which increases attenuation. Cables in the CENTER, with the worst airflow, are affected most. Mitigation: use Cat6A (better heat dissipation), follow bundle-size deratings, and favor ventilated trays over sealed conduits.
encounters.question: A building installs 200 PoE+ security cameras (802.3bt, ~60W each), with all cables run together in a single large bundle inside a sealed conduit. After a few months, cameras in the CENTER of the bundle show intermittent connectivity and higher-than-expected attenuation on cable certification tests, while cables on the OUTER edge of the bundle test fine. What is the most likely cause, and what would help?
options: The center cables are simply longer than the outer cables, exceeding the 100m limit

Cumulative heat from high-wattage PoE+ current across hundreds of bundled cables raises the temperature inside the bundle, especially in the center where airflow is worst; higher temperature increases copper resistance and attenuation. Using Cat6A and following bundle-size deratings or improving airflow would help
PoE+ cameras require fiber, not copper, so copper cabling will always fail eventually
The issue is unrelated to PoE — it must be EMI from fluorescent lighting near the conduit
encounters.explanation: Heat from current through hundreds of bundled PoE+ cables accumulates inside a sealed bundle, hitting center cables hardest where airflow is worst. Heat raises copper resistance, which directly increases attenuation — exactly the certification failures described, isolated to the center. Cat6A's larger conductors dissipate heat better; bundle-size deratings and better airflow reduce the buildup. Wrong: (A) cable length is per-run, unrelated to position-in-bundle. (C) PoE+ over copper is standard up to 100m at full power. (D) EMI from lighting correlates with proximity to fixtures, not center-vs-edge bundle position.

encounters.question: Which tool is used to locate the far end of an unknown cable by injecting an audio tone and tracing it?
options: OTDR
Cable certifier
Toner generator and probe (fox and hound)
Loopback adapter
encounters.explanation: A toner generator and probe (fox and hound): the generator injects an audio tone at one end; the probe detects the tone at the other end — allowing you to trace unlabelled cables through walls, ceilings, and cable bundles.

encounters.question: An OTDR is used primarily for troubleshooting:
options: Copper Ethernet cable faults
Wi-Fi channel interference
Fiber optic cables — locating breaks and measuring loss
Power supply issues in network equipment
encounters.explanation: OTDR (Optical Time Domain Reflectometer) sends a light pulse into fiber and measures backscattered/reflected light to locate faults, breaks, and splices — reporting the exact distance to each event. Essential for fiber troubleshooting.

encounters.question: A straight-through Ethernet cable is used to connect:
options: Switch to switch (same device type)
PC to PC directly
PC to switch (different device types)
Router console port to laptop
encounters.explanation: Straight-through cable: same pinout (T568B or T568A) on both ends — used to connect DIFFERENT device types (PC → switch, switch → router). Crossover cable: different standards on each end — used to connect SAME device types (PC → PC, switch → switch). MDI/MDIX on modern equipment auto-corrects this.

encounters.question: T568A and T568B wiring standards differ in which way?
options: They use completely different pin assignments
Orange and green pairs are swapped between the two standards
T568A uses Cat5e; T568B uses Cat6
They use different connector types
encounters.explanation: T568A and T568B differ only in that the orange pair (pins 1,2) and green pair (pins 3,6) are swapped. Both are valid — but you must use the SAME standard on both ends of a straight-through cable. A crossover cable uses T568A on one end and T568B on the other.

encounters.question: A loopback adapter is used to:
options: Bridge two network segments
Test a port by connecting TX to RX — verifies the port's send and receive hardware
Convert between fiber and copper
Capture traffic on a port for analysis
encounters.explanation: A loopback adapter connects the transmit pin to the receive pin on a port. Traffic sent by the port is immediately received back. If the loopback test passes, the port hardware is functional — isolating the issue to the cable or remote device.

encounters.question: A cable passes a basic continuity test but shows excessive errors at Gigabit speeds. What fault is most likely?
options: Open circuit on one pair
Split pair — wires from different pairs crossed — passes continuity but causes crosstalk
Cable too short
Wrong connector type
encounters.explanation: Split pairs: a wire from pair 2 and a wire from pair 3 are used together instead of the correct pair. The basic continuity test (all 8 pins connected) passes, but the untwisted wires generate high crosstalk (NEXT) at Gigabit speeds. A wire map tester with pair identification catches this.

encounters.question: CRC errors are increasing on a switch interface after a new cable was installed. What should you check FIRST?
options: VLAN configuration
The new cable and its connectors — bad crimping or damaged cable causes CRC errors
Spanning tree topology
DHCP lease table
encounters.explanation: CRC errors indicate corrupt frames — most commonly caused by physical layer issues: bad cable, loose connector, poor crimping, damaged SFP transceiver, or EMI interference. New cable + new CRC errors = strong indicator to replace/re-crimp the cable first.

encounters.question: What is attenuation in a cable, and when does it become a problem?
options: Voltage fluctuations caused by power surges — only a problem near generators
Signal loss as it travels along the cable — becomes a problem beyond the cable's rated distance
Interference between cables — only occurs in unshielded cables
Incorrect impedance matching — only relevant for coaxial cable
encounters.explanation: Attenuation is the weakening of signal over distance. For copper Ethernet (Cat5e/6), the limit is 100m total channel. Beyond that, signal degrades below usable levels — errors increase, speed drops, link may fail. Fiber has much lower attenuation and can run kilometres.

encounters.question: A rollover cable (console cable) connects which two things?
options: Two switches for inter-VLAN routing
PC/laptop serial/USB port to router or switch console port for management
Two patch panels in the same rack
Fiber equipment to copper Ethernet
encounters.explanation: Rollover cables (Cisco console cables) have pins completely reversed (pin 1↔8, 2↔7, etc.) — they look like a flat grey cable. Used ONLY for out-of-band management access to the router/switch console port. Not used for data connectivity.

encounters.question: Which tool would best identify whether an existing fiber cable run meets the loss budget for 10GbE at 300m?
options: Cable continuity tester
Toner probe
Optical power meter and light source (or OTDR)
Spectrum analyser
encounters.explanation: An optical power meter measures the actual optical signal strength (dBm) at the far end of the fiber. Compare received power against the transmitter's output power — the difference is the insertion loss. If within budget, the link will work. OTDR provides a detailed loss profile including splice and connector losses.

encounters.question: A switch port shows high input errors and runts. The remote device is a server with a NIC set to full-duplex 1Gbps. The switch port is set to auto-negotiate. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cable is too long
Duplex mismatch — auto-negotiate may settle at half-duplex if the NIC forces full-duplex without advertising
The server NIC is faulty
The switch VLAN configuration is wrong
encounters.explanation: When one side forces full-duplex and the other auto-negotiates: the auto-negotiating switch port may fall back to half-duplex (no duplex info received). Result: server sends full-duplex, switch expects half-duplex CSMA/CD — collisions, runts, CRC errors on the switch side. Fix: set both sides explicitly to the same duplex and speed.

encounters.question: EMI (Electromagnetic Interference) on a copper cable run can be mitigated by:
options: Increasing cable bandwidth category (Cat5e to Cat6)
Running the cable parallel to power cables for maximum proximity
Using shielded cable (STP/FTP) and routing away from high-EMI sources; crossing power cables at 90 degrees
Reducing cable length to under 50m
encounters.explanation: EMI mitigation for copper cable: (1) use shielded cable (STP/FTP) near motors, fluorescent lights, power cables — shield must be properly grounded; (2) route data cables away from power cables; (3) where crossing is unavoidable, cross at 90 degrees to minimise coupling; (4) use fiber optic cable (immune to EMI) in high-interference environments.

encounters.question: A punch-down tool is used when:
options: Testing cable continuity
Terminating copper cable into a patch panel or keystone jack (110 block / 66 block)
Tracing cables through walls
Measuring optical signal strength
encounters.explanation: A punch-down tool seats individual wires into IDC (Insulation Displacement Connector) slots on 110-type patch panels and keystone jacks. It simultaneously inserts the wire and cuts off the excess — correct seating is critical for cable performance.

encounters.question: A fiber link passes an optical power meter test (loss within budget) but the interface still doesn't come up. What should you check next?
options: Replace the fiber with copper
Check TX/RX polarity — fiber has separate transmit and receive strands that may be swapped
The cable is too short
Replace the entire patch panel
encounters.explanation: Fiber links use separate strands for TX and RX. If TX on one end connects to TX on the other (instead of RX), the link cannot come up regardless of optical power. Check that the patch cable and cassette are wired TX→RX on both ends (straight-through vs crossover polarity). This is a common installation mistake.

nodes.name: The Command Post
nodes.description: Network troubleshooting commands — ping, traceroute, nslookup, nmap, netstat, arp, ipconfig.

encounters.title: The Phone Call That Hangs Up Mid-Sentence
encounters.scenario: Imagine you're on a phone call and the line suddenly goes dead mid-sentence — from YOUR side, all you know is 'the call ended.' A TCP RST (reset) is exactly that: one side immediately tears down the connection without the normal goodbye (FIN/ACK) handshake. From the CLIENT's view ('Connection reset'), you can't tell WHO hung up or WHY — the server crashing? a firewall actively terminating it? nothing listening on that port? A PACKET CAPTURE (tcpdump/Wireshark) at multiple points reveals the picture: the SOURCE IP of the RST (the server, or a middle device spoofing it?), where it falls in the sequence, and timing. Capturing at BOTH ends can expose discrepancies — like a RST the receiver sees but the sender never sent.
encounters.question: Users report connections to an internal app server (port 8443) get abruptly reset a few seconds after connecting. A technician runs tcpdump simultaneously at the client and the server. The server-side capture shows SYN, SYN-ACK, and several data packets — but the server NEVER sends a RST. The client-side capture shows a RST arriving with a source IP matching the server. What does this discrepancy most likely indicate, and what should the technician check next?
options: The server's NIC is faulty and dropping its own outgoing RST packets before they reach the capture

An intermediate device (firewall, IPS, or load balancer) on the path is injecting a RST with a spoofed source IP to terminate the connection — likely a security policy, idle timeout, or inspection rule; check inline security device logs/policies for that connection
TCP RST packets are never visible in packet captures — the client must be misreading a FIN packet as a RST
The client's OS generated the RST locally due to a timeout, and the source IP shown in a capture is irrelevant
encounters.explanation: If the server's own capture shows it never sent a RST, but the client received one appearing to be FROM the server, that RST was injected ON THE PATH — classic behavior of an inline security appliance terminating a connection by sending a spoofed RST, which looks to the receiver exactly like the other side hung up. This is why multi-point captures matter — they surface discrepancies a single capture would hide. Wrong: (A) a NIC dropping its OWN outgoing packets wouldn't explain the CLIENT receiving a RST from somewhere on the wire. (C) RST is a normal flag, distinct from FIN, in any capture. (D) a client-generated RST would carry the CLIENT's source IP, not the server's.

encounters.title: The Guest List vs the Building Directory
encounters.scenario: A switch's MAC ADDRESS TABLE is a guest list at a building's front desk: it records which ROOM (port) each VISITOR (MAC address) is in, learned automatically as frames arrive. 'show mac address-table' tells you 'MAC AA:BB:CC is on port Gi0/3' — great for finding WHERE an end device connects. But it says nothing about which hallways connect to OTHER buildings (switches/routers). CDP/LLDP is a directory shared between adjacent buildings' front desks: each device periodically announces itself (name, model, IP, port) to its directly-connected neighbors. 'show cdp/lldp neighbors' tells you 'Gi0/24 here connects to Gi0/1 on SwitchB' — mapping topology between infrastructure devices, not where end-user devices sit.
encounters.question: A technician needs to find (1) which physical switch port a user's laptop (known MAC address) is plugged into, AND (2) how that access switch connects upstream to the distribution switch (which port-to-port link). Which combination of commands provides this, and why can't either alone do the whole job?
options: show mac address-table alone provides both, since MAC addresses uniquely identify both end devices and switches

show mac address-table (to find which port the laptop's MAC is learned on) plus show cdp/lldp neighbors (to find which port connects to the distribution switch and which port it terminates on there) — the MAC table maps end-host locations, while CDP/LLDP maps inter-device topology
show cdp neighbors alone provides both, since CDP tracks every MAC address on every port, including end-user devices
Neither command can provide this — only a physical site walk-through with a cable tracer can determine port-to-port connections
encounters.explanation: The MAC table is built from frames received — it records which port each source MAC was last seen on, exactly how you find an end-host's port. CDP/LLDP is separate: devices announce themselves to direct neighbors, revealing device-to-device topology that a MAC table doesn't show. Wrong: (A) two switches don't exchange identity via MAC entries — an uplink port just shows a pile of OTHER devices' MACs learned through it. (C) CDP/LLDP isn't typically supported on end-user devices — it's for infrastructure links. (D) CDP/LLDP exists specifically to avoid physical cable tracing — both commands are standard, fast tools.

encounters.question: What does a 169.254.x.x IP address in ipconfig output indicate?
options: A valid static IP assigned by the admin
A public IP assigned by the ISP
APIPA — the host failed to obtain a DHCP address and self-assigned a link-local address
An IPv6 link-local address
encounters.explanation: 169.254.x.x is APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) — assigned by Windows/macOS when DHCP fails. The host cannot reach other networks with this address (link-local only). Fix: resolve the DHCP issue (server down, scope exhausted, cable unplugged).

encounters.question: The traceroute / tracert command is used to:
options: Test if a remote host is reachable
Show the hop-by-hop path packets take to a destination and the RTT at each hop
Display the local routing table
Scan open ports on a remote host
encounters.explanation: Traceroute/tracert uses incrementing TTL values to discover each router hop between source and destination. It shows RTT at each hop and where packets stop — useful for identifying where connectivity fails or latency is introduced.

encounters.question: What command would you use to test DNS resolution on a Windows machine?
options: ping
tracert
nslookup
netstat
encounters.explanation: nslookup (or dig on Linux/macOS) queries DNS servers and displays the results — showing which DNS server responded, the resolved IP, and any errors (NXDOMAIN = name not found). Essential for DNS troubleshooting.

encounters.question: What does 'ping 127.0.0.1' test?
options: Connectivity to the default gateway
Connectivity to the DNS server
The local TCP/IP stack — loopback address
Whether the NIC has a cable connected
encounters.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address — it tests the local TCP/IP stack without requiring a network interface or cable. If this fails, the TCP/IP stack itself is broken (reinstall TCP/IP stack). If this passes but other pings fail, the issue is external to the host.

encounters.question: The arp -a command displays:
options: The local routing table
The DNS cache
The ARP cache — IP-to-MAC address mappings learned by the local host
Open network ports and connections
encounters.explanation: arp -a shows the ARP cache — the local table mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses. Useful for detecting ARP poisoning (same IP mapped to two different MACs), duplicate IPs, or confirming the gateway resolves to the correct MAC.

encounters.question: traceroute shows '* * *' at a particular hop. What does this mean?
options: The link at that hop is down
That router does not respond to ICMP TTL-exceeded messages — but traffic may still be forwarded
The destination is unreachable
Packet loss is 100% at that hop
encounters.explanation: '* * *' means no ICMP TTL-exceeded response was received from that hop. Many routers are configured not to respond to ICMP messages (rate limiting or ACL). This does NOT necessarily mean the link is broken — if subsequent hops respond, traffic is still flowing through it.

encounters.question: pathping (Windows) is more useful than tracert because it:
options: Uses TCP instead of ICMP
Combines tracert path discovery with per-hop packet loss statistics over multiple samples
Resolves hostnames faster
Can bypass firewall restrictions
encounters.explanation: pathping sends multiple packets to each hop and calculates packet loss percentage per hop — identifying exactly which hop is dropping packets. tracert shows RTT only for a single sample. pathping takes longer but provides more diagnostic information for intermittent issues.

encounters.question: nmap is used for which troubleshooting/security task?
options: Capturing full packet payloads
Network discovery and port scanning — identifying live hosts and open ports/services
Displaying local ARP cache
Measuring optical fiber signal loss
encounters.explanation: nmap (Network Mapper) performs host discovery (which hosts are alive) and port scanning (which ports are open/filtered/closed) and service/OS detection. Used for network inventory, vulnerability assessment, and confirming firewall rules are working.

encounters.question: On a Cisco switch, 'show interface Gi0/1' shows 'input errors: 1240, CRC: 1240'. What should you investigate?
options: VLAN configuration on the port
The physical cable and connector between this port and the connected device
The spanning tree state of the port
The DHCP lease table
encounters.explanation: Input CRC errors on a Cisco interface = corrupt frames arriving — physical layer problem. Check: the cable (replace it), the patch panel termination, the connector crimping, and the SFP/transceiver. Also check for duplex mismatch (late collisions often accompany CRC in that case).

encounters.question: What does 'netstat -an' display?
options: The ARP cache with MAC addresses
All active TCP/UDP connections and listening ports with numeric addresses (no DNS resolution)
The local routing table
Interface IP configuration
encounters.explanation: netstat -an shows all active connections (ESTABLISHED) and listening ports (LISTENING) in numeric format (-n skips DNS reverse lookup for speed). Useful for identifying which services are listening, detecting unexpected connections, and confirming a service started on the correct port.

encounters.question: ipconfig /flushdns clears the local DNS resolver cache. When should you use this?
options: After changing a NIC driver
When a DNS record has been updated but the host still resolves the old IP (stale cache)
After changing the default gateway
When APIPA is assigned
encounters.explanation: Windows caches DNS responses for their TTL. If a DNS record is updated (server IP changed, domain moved), clients still resolve the old IP until their cache expires. ipconfig /flushdns forces immediate re-query of DNS for all names.

encounters.question: On a router, 'show ip route' shows no default route (0.0.0.0/0). What connectivity impact does this have?
options: No impact — directly connected routes still work
Only traffic to directly connected networks will be routed — all other traffic is dropped (no internet)
Only OSPF routes will fail
DNS queries will fail
encounters.explanation: Without a default route (gateway of last resort), the router drops any packet destined for a network not in its routing table. For internet access, a default route pointing to the ISP is essential. Hosts behind this router lose all non-local connectivity.

encounters.question: Which command on a Windows host would show the local IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server addresses?
options: netstat
arp -a
ipconfig /all
route print
encounters.explanation: ipconfig /all shows complete NIC configuration: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server addresses, MAC address, DHCP lease information, and whether DHCP or static IP is used. The '/all' flag is essential — plain 'ipconfig' omits DNS and MAC.

encounters.question: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 but not www.google.com. nslookup www.google.com returns 'DNS request timed out'. What is the problem?
options: The IP route to Google is broken
The DNS server configured on the host is unreachable or not responding
The TLS certificate for Google is expired
The default gateway is wrong
encounters.explanation: Ping to 8.8.8.8 works = IP routing fine. nslookup timeout = the DNS server (not 8.8.8.8 apparently — or 8.8.8.8 is unreachable via UDP 53) is not responding. Check: ipconfig /all to see which DNS server is configured, then ping that server. If that DNS server is unreachable, fix DNS server config or firewall rules for UDP 53.

nodes.name: The Signal Tower
nodes.description: Wireless troubleshooting — interference, coverage, authentication failures, and APIPA.

encounters.title: The Highway Lanes: 2.4GHz vs 5GHz vs 6GHz
encounters.scenario: 2.4GHz is an old, narrow backroad everyone uses — microwaves, Bluetooth, baby monitors, and neighboring APs crowd onto it, with only 3 non-overlapping channels (1/6/11). But its lower frequency travels FARTHER and penetrates walls better. 5GHz is a wider highway with 24+ non-overlapping channels and wider channels (40/80/160MHz) — far less congestion and higher throughput, but shorter range. 6GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7) is a near-empty new freeway — 59 non-overlapping channels, least congestion, highest throughput potential, but the SHORTEST range of the three. Rule of thumb: as frequency goes UP, range/penetration goes DOWN, but available spectrum and throughput potential go UP.
encounters.question: A multi-floor office has two complaints: (1) users in a large open warehouse far from any AP report weak, dropping signal, and (2) users in a densely-packed engineering area near many APs report slow speeds despite strong signal, with spectrum analysis showing heavy channel overlap. An engineer proposes moving warehouse clients toward 2.4GHz and engineering-area clients toward 5GHz/6GHz. Does this make sense?
options: No — frequency band has no effect on range or congestion; the issue must be AP hardware age in both cases

Yes — 2.4GHz's lower frequency travels farther and penetrates obstacles better, helping the warehouse's range problem; 5GHz/6GHz offer far more non-overlapping channels and wider-bandwidth options, reducing the congestion/overlap causing the engineering area's slowdowns
No — 6GHz should be used in the warehouse, because higher frequencies always have the longest range
Yes, but only because 2.4GHz devices are inherently newer and faster than 5GHz devices
encounters.explanation: Frequency affects both propagation physics and available spectrum — 2.4GHz's longer wavelength gives better range/penetration, useful where coverage (not speed) is the bottleneck, despite only 3 channels. 5GHz (24+) and 6GHz (59 channels) provide far more spectrum to spread dense deployments without overlap, addressing congestion, at the cost of range. Wrong: (A) this range-vs-channels tradeoff IS the core effect of frequency. (C) reverses it — 6GHz has the SHORTEST range of the three, the worst choice for a sparse warehouse. (D) 2.4GHz isn't 'faster' or 'newer' — 5GHz/6GHz support wider channels and higher throughput; the conclusion in B is right, but for range/channel reasons, not device age.

encounters.title: The Lantern, the Flashlight, and the Laser Pointer
encounters.scenario: An OMNIDIRECTIONAL antenna is a LANTERN: light spreads 360° horizontally — great for general coverage in an open area (a typical indoor AP), but energy is spread thin, limiting range in any one direction. A DIRECTIONAL antenna (Yagi/patch) is a FLASHLIGHT: it focuses energy into a beam toward one direction, giving higher gain along that path — useful for a hallway or a medium-distance point-to-point link. A PARABOLIC DISH is a LASER POINTER: an extremely narrow, very high-gain beam for LONG-DISTANCE PtP links — connecting buildings across a campus or miles apart, where all energy must aim precisely at the other dish. For a PtP bridge you need high gain and a narrow beam aimed at the other end; an omni wastes nearly all its energy where there's no receiver.
encounters.question: A company needs to bridge a warehouse network to a main office network 1.5 miles away, with clear rooftop-to-rooftop line-of-sight. They install standard omnidirectional antennas on wireless bridges at both ends, but the link is unreliable with very low throughput. What change would most likely fix this, and why?
options: Replace the omnidirectional antennas with high-gain directional antennas (parabolic dish or high-gain Yagi) aimed precisely at each other — concentrating the radio energy into a narrow, high-gain beam toward the only receiver that matters, instead of spreading it 360°
Increase the transmit power on the omnidirectional antennas — power output, not antenna pattern, determines point-to-point link quality
Switch both ends to 2.4GHz, since lower frequencies are always better for long-distance links regardless of antenna type
1.5 miles is simply impossible for any wireless technology — a fiber run is the only solution
encounters.explanation: Omni antennas spread energy 360° — for a PtP link, only a tiny fraction reaches the other end, while the antenna receives interference equally from every direction. A directional antenna concentrates the SAME transmit power into a narrow beam aimed at the other end, dramatically increasing received signal while reducing interference — exactly what long-distance PtP requires. Wrong: (B) an omni at higher power still wastes most power in useless directions, and EIRP limits cap this anyway — antenna pattern, not raw power, is the key lever. (C) 2.4GHz isn't 'always better'; many PtP bridges run on 5GHz with directional antennas — the antenna mismatch is the root cause. (D) 1.5-mile PtP bridges with directional antennas and clear LOS are common and well-established.

encounters.question: A laptop connected to Wi-Fi shows IP address 169.254.47.12. What does this indicate?
options: Excellent Wi-Fi signal — the AP assigned a link-local address
Successful WPA3 authentication
DHCP failure — Wi-Fi connected but could not obtain a DHCP address
The MAC address was blocked by wireless ACL
encounters.explanation: 169.254.x.x (APIPA) means the device connected to the Wi-Fi network successfully at Layer 2 but failed to get a DHCP address (DHCP server down, scope exhausted, or DHCP relay misconfigured). The Wi-Fi association itself worked — this is a DHCP/Layer 3 issue.

encounters.question: A user's Wi-Fi disconnects every time the office microwave is used. What is the cause?
options: The AP needs a firmware update
Microwave interference — microwave ovens emit 2.4 GHz RF in the same band as 802.11b/g/n
The user's Wi-Fi password is being reset
Co-channel interference from a neighbouring AP
encounters.explanation: Microwave ovens emit wideband RF energy in the 2.4 GHz ISM band — overlapping with 802.11b/g/n Wi-Fi. When the microwave runs, it raises the noise floor and causes disconnections. Fix: connect the client to a 5 GHz SSID (802.11ac or 5GHz 802.11n), which is unaffected by microwave ovens.

encounters.question: A user cannot find their corporate Wi-Fi SSID even though other users nearby can. What is the most likely cause?
options: The user's device is banned from the wireless network
The user's device only supports 5 GHz but the SSID is broadcast on 2.4 GHz only, or the device is too far from the AP
The AP has been deauthenticated
The SSID uses WPA3 which the device doesn't support
encounters.explanation: If others can see the SSID but one user cannot: (1) device may only support one band and the SSID is on the other band, (2) device is at the edge of coverage range while others are closer, (3) device's Wi-Fi adapter is disabled, or (4) the device driver has a compatibility issue.

encounters.question: An office has three APs all on channel 6 of the 2.4 GHz band. Users experience slow speeds. What is the problem?
options: The gateway is overloaded
Co-channel interference — all APs sharing channel 6 compete for airtime
The SSIDs are broadcasting on different channels
WPA2 authentication is too slow
encounters.explanation: Co-channel interference: multiple APs on the same channel must take turns transmitting (CSMA/CA). The more APs on a channel, the more contention — resulting in lower throughput per client. Fix: assign APs to non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11) so each AP has its own channel.

encounters.question: A new employee cannot connect to the corporate Wi-Fi. They receive an 'Authentication Failed' error. What should you check first?
options: The AP firmware version
Whether the passphrase (PSK) entered is correct and that WPA2 vs WPA3 client settings match the AP
The DHCP scope
Whether the corporate switch has the correct VLAN
encounters.explanation: Authentication failed = credentials problem. First check: correct PSK (case-sensitive), correct security type (WPA2-PSK vs WPA3-SAE vs WPA2-Enterprise). If Enterprise: check RADIUS reachability, correct username/password, valid certificate.

encounters.question: Users in a conference room far from the nearest AP complain of poor Wi-Fi performance despite showing 'connected'. What is the issue?
options: The SSID password is wrong for that room
Weak signal / low RSSI — AP too far away; client transmits at low MCS rate to compensate for weak signal
The AP is overheating
Co-channel interference is too high
encounters.explanation: 802.11 rate adaptation: as signal weakens (distance increases), the client/AP automatically uses lower, more robust modulation rates (e.g., drops from 802.11ac 433Mbps to 802.11n 54Mbps or lower). User stays 'connected' but at a fraction of the potential speed. Fix: add an AP or extend coverage.

encounters.question: A user on WPA2 Enterprise fails to authenticate. They receive a certificate error. What is most likely wrong?
options: Wrong PSK entered
RADIUS server certificate is expired, untrusted, or the client is not configured to trust the CA that signed the RADIUS cert
The DHCP scope is exhausted
The AP's channel is congested
encounters.explanation: WPA2 Enterprise with PEAP or EAP-TLS: the client validates the RADIUS server's certificate. If the cert is expired, self-signed and untrusted, or the CA is not in the device's trust store — authentication fails with a certificate error. Fix: renew cert, install CA cert on clients, or update client EAP profile.

encounters.question: After deploying a new LWAP, it won't appear in the WLC. What should you check?
options: Whether the AP is within range of other APs
Whether the AP received an IP from DHCP and whether it can reach the WLC on UDP 5246/5247 (CAPWAP)
Whether the AP's channel is set correctly
Whether the AP's SSID password is configured
encounters.explanation: LWAP boot process: (1) gets DHCP address (option 43 may provide WLC IP), (2) discovers WLC via CAPWAP on UDP 5246/5247, (3) downloads config from WLC. If AP doesn't appear in WLC: check DHCP (has the AP got an IP?), check CAPWAP reachability (firewall blocking?), check WLC AP licence.

encounters.question: A spectrum analyser shows a constant wide-band noise source at 2.4 GHz that isn't a Wi-Fi signal. What is a likely source?
options: A misconfigured SSID
A malfunctioning or leaking microwave oven, or a cordless phone operating in the 2.4 GHz band
A rogue access point on channel 6
Bluetooth pairing traffic
encounters.explanation: Non-802.11 interference appears on a spectrum analyser as non-channel-shaped noise. Wide-band continuous 2.4 GHz interference = microwave oven (when cooking). Pulsed 2.4 GHz = cordless phones. Frequency-hopping = Bluetooth or ZigBee. A rogue AP would look like a proper 802.11 signal.

encounters.question: A user connects to Wi-Fi but can only reach local network resources — not the internet. Other users on the same AP have internet access. What is the most likely cause specific to this user's device?
options: The AP DHCP scope is exhausted
The user's device has a manually configured incorrect default gateway or DNS server
The AP is overloaded with too many clients
The 5 GHz band is saturated
encounters.explanation: If other users on the same AP have internet access, the AP/DHCP/routing are all working. The problem is specific to this device: likely a manually configured wrong default gateway or wrong DNS server (overriding DHCP-provided settings). Check: ipconfig /all — is the gateway correct? Is DNS correct?

encounters.question: During a VoIP call, a user walks between two APs and the call drops. Coverage overlap was measured at 10%. What is wrong?
options: The user's device does not support 802.11r
Insufficient cell overlap — 10% is too low for seamless roaming. Minimum ~15-20% overlap required for clients to associate with the new AP before losing the old one
The user's device is on the wrong VLAN
WPA3 SAE takes too long to re-authenticate
encounters.explanation: Wireless roaming requires sufficient cell overlap (~15-20%) so the client can discover and pre-authenticate with the new AP before the old AP signal drops too low. With 10% overlap, the client loses the first AP before associating with the second — causing the call drop. Fix: increase AP power or add an AP.

encounters.question: Hidden SSID (not broadcasting the network name) is considered weak security because:
options: It prevents devices from connecting at all
Clients must broadcast probe requests for the hidden SSID — attackers can see the network name in these probe frames
Hidden SSIDs cannot use WPA2 encryption
The AP becomes visible to all devices when broadcasting
encounters.explanation: Hiding the SSID only removes it from beacon frames. Clients that know the SSID actively probe for it — sending the SSID name in clear text in probe request frames. Any passive RF monitor can capture these and learn the hidden SSID. It provides no meaningful security benefit and causes connection issues.

encounters.question: A network admin notices multiple clients rapidly disconnecting and reconnecting to the corporate AP. What attack is most likely occurring?
options: ARP poisoning attack on the LAN
Deauthentication (deauth) flood attack — attacker sends spoofed deauth frames forcing clients off the AP
DHCP starvation — client IPs are being stolen
STP topology change causing MAC table flush
encounters.explanation: Deauth flood: attacker sends a continuous stream of spoofed 802.11 deauthentication management frames (no auth required in WPA2 without 802.11w) — clients continuously disconnect. Mitigation: enable 802.11w (Management Frame Protection) which requires management frames to be cryptographically authenticated.

nodes.name: The Service Desk
nodes.description: DHCP, DNS, NTP, routing, duplicate IP, and IP addressing service troubleshooting.

encounters.title: The Phonebook's Different Page Types: DNS Records
encounters.scenario: DNS is a phonebook with different PAGE TYPES. An A record = 'Name → IPv4 address,' the basic white-pages entry. AAAA = the same for IPv6. CNAME = 'this name is just an ALIAS — look up THIS OTHER name instead.' MX (Mail Exchanger) = 'for THIS domain's email, deliver to THIS mail server,' with a priority (lower = preferred). TXT = a free-form notes field, used for ownership verification and email security (SPF/DKIM/DMARC). NS = 'THESE servers are authoritative for this domain.' PTR = a REVERSE lookup, IP → name. SRV = 'for THIS service, connect to THIS host on THIS port,' used by VoIP/directory auto-discovery.
encounters.question: A company stands up a new mail server and creates an A record (mail.example.com → new IP), but forgets to update the MX record, which still points to 'oldmail.example.com' — a name with no A record at all. Separately, the PTR record for the new mail server's IP still resolves back to the OLD server's hostname. What are the likely consequences of EACH issue?
options: Both are cosmetic only — DNS records are purely for human readability with no functional impact

The stale MX record means inbound email can't be delivered (other mail servers can't find a valid destination via 'oldmail.example.com'); the mismatched PTR record can get outbound mail flagged as spam, since many receiving servers check that the sending IP's PTR hostname matches the sender (forward-confirmed reverse DNS)
Both issues only affect IPv6 connectivity — IPv4 mail delivery is unaffected by MX or PTR records
The MX record issue is irrelevant because A records alone are sufficient for email delivery; only the PTR record matters
encounters.explanation: MX records tell other mail servers WHERE to deliver mail for a domain — if it points to a hostname with no A/AAAA record, inbound mail fails entirely, no matter how correct the new server's own A record is. PTR records (reverse DNS) are checked by many receiving servers as part of spam filtering — a mismatch between a sending IP's PTR hostname and the actual sender (FCrDNS) can get outbound mail flagged. Wrong: (A) MX and PTR have direct functional consequences, not just informational ones. (C) these are application-layer (DNS/SMTP) concerns, independent of IPv4 vs IPv6. (D) an A record only resolves a name once you know which name to look up — that's the MX record's job.

encounters.title: The Translator Who Forwards Your Shout Across the River
encounters.scenario: DHCP DISCOVER messages are BROADCASTS (255.255.255.255), and routers don't forward broadcasts between subnets/VLANs by design — staying within one broadcast domain is the whole point of segmenting with VLANs. So a client on VLAN 30 shouting 'DHCP DISCOVER!' can't be heard by a DHCP server on VLAN 1 — the router silently drops the broadcast. A DHCP RELAY AGENT (configured via 'ip helper-address <server IP>' on the VLAN 30 SVI) is a translator at the river's edge: it hears the broadcast on VLAN 30 and repackages it as a UNICAST packet to the DHCP server, stamping its own interface IP into the GIADDR field — telling the server 'this came from VLAN 30, use that scope, and send the reply back to ME to relay.'
encounters.question: A new VLAN 30 (subnet 10.30.0.0/24) is created on a Layer 3 switch. Devices plugged into VLAN 30 receive APIPA (169.254.x.x) addresses instead of addresses from the central DHCP server, which lives on VLAN 1 and already has a configured scope for 10.30.0.0/24. What is the most likely missing configuration, and how does it work?
options: The DHCP server needs a second network card physically connected to VLAN 30

An 'ip helper-address' (DHCP relay) pointing to the central DHCP server is missing on VLAN 30's SVI — without it, DHCP DISCOVER broadcasts from VLAN 30 never cross the router boundary; the relay converts the broadcast to a unicast packet addressed to the server, tagging it with the VLAN 30 gateway's IP so the server picks the correct scope
VLAN 30 needs its own separate DHCP server — a single DHCP server can never serve more than one subnet, even with relay configured
The clients need static routes manually configured pointing to the DHCP server
encounters.explanation: DHCP DISCOVER is a broadcast, and routers don't forward broadcasts between subnets by design. An 'ip helper-address' on the VLAN 30 SVI listens for DHCP broadcasts and relays them as unicast to the configured server, including the GIADDR so the server picks the right scope and knows where to reply. Wrong: (A) one server can serve many subnets/scopes — that's the point of relay. (C) one centrally-located server with multiple scopes is standard, made possible by relay. (D) clients can't have static routes before they HAVE an IP — this is a Layer 2/3 issue solved by relay.

encounters.question: New devices on the network are failing to get IP addresses. Existing devices work fine. What is the most likely DHCP cause?
options: DHCP is disabled
DNS is down
DHCP scope exhaustion — all available IPs in the pool are already assigned
The default gateway is unreachable
encounters.explanation: When existing devices work (they already have leases) but new devices cannot get IPs, the DHCP scope is typically exhausted — all available addresses are leased. Fix: expand the scope, reduce lease time, or clean up stale leases from disconnected devices.

encounters.question: A user can ping IPs but cannot reach websites by name. ipconfig /all shows DNS: 192.168.1.50 but that server is offline. What is the fix?
options: Replace the network cable
Correct the DNS server address — point to a working DNS server (either manually or via DHCP option 6)
Enable DHCP on the interface
Renew the IP address with ipconfig /release /renew
encounters.explanation: IP works but DNS fails = wrong or unreachable DNS server. The quickest fix: update the DHCP scope's DNS option (option 6) to point to a working DNS server, then renew client leases. Or manually set a working DNS server (8.8.8.8 temporarily for testing).

encounters.question: Two workstations have been manually configured with the same IP address. What symptom will users experience?
options: Both machines have double the network speed
Neither machine may function reliably on the network — ARP conflicts cause intermittent connectivity
Only one machine works; the other is blocked
The switch disables both ports for security
encounters.explanation: Duplicate IP addresses cause ARP conflicts — both machines respond to ARP requests for that IP. Traffic destined for that IP gets routed to whichever machine responded last, causing intermittent failures for both. Some operating systems also display a duplicate IP warning. Fix: assign unique static IPs or use DHCP.

encounters.question: A host can reach other devices on its local subnet but cannot reach any remote networks. The default gateway is set to 0.0.0.0. What is wrong?
options: The DNS server is unreachable
No default gateway configured — without a gateway, the host cannot send traffic off the local subnet
The subnet mask is wrong
The NIC driver needs updating
encounters.explanation: The default gateway tells the host where to send packets destined for networks it doesn't have a direct route to. Without it (0.0.0.0 or blank), traffic to remote networks is dropped locally. Fix: configure the correct default gateway (usually the router's LAN interface IP).

encounters.question: NTP (Network Time Protocol) time synchronisation failure can cause which serious problem?
options: Slower internet speeds
Kerberos authentication failures — Active Directory requires clocks within 5 minutes of each other
DHCP scope exhaustion
DNS NXDOMAIN errors
encounters.explanation: Kerberos (used in Active Directory/Windows authentication) requires all clocks to be within 5 minutes of each other. If time skew exceeds this, authentication fails — users cannot log in, access shares, or authenticate to domain resources. NTP uses UDP port 123.

encounters.question: A host at 192.168.1.10/24 cannot communicate with another host at 192.168.1.200/25. The admin claims they're on the same network. What is the problem?
options: The hosts need static routes to each other
Subnet mask mismatch — one host uses /24, the other /25. They calculate different network ranges and cannot communicate directly
The switch needs VLANs configured
DNS is resolving to incorrect IPs
encounters.explanation: /24 = network 192.168.1.0 with range .1–.254. /25 = network 192.168.1.128 with range .129–.254. The /25 host calculates that the /24 host (192.168.1.10) is on a DIFFERENT network and sends it to the default gateway instead of direct ARP. The /24 host does the opposite — sends direct. This asymmetric routing breaks communication.

encounters.question: nslookup returns 'NXDOMAIN' for a new server hostname. What does this mean?
options: The DNS server is offline
The hostname does not exist in DNS — the DNS record was not created
The hostname resolves to the wrong IP
The DNS cache needs flushing
encounters.explanation: NXDOMAIN (Non-Existent Domain) means the queried hostname doesn't exist in DNS at all — no A/AAAA record found. The DNS server responded but couldn't find the record. Fix: create the missing DNS record for the new server. Different from a timeout (server unreachable) or wrong IP (wrong record value).

encounters.question: A DHCP server is configured with option 3 set to 192.168.1.1, but the actual router's LAN IP is 192.168.1.254. Users cannot reach the internet. What is the root cause?
options: The DHCP scope has no available addresses
DHCP option 3 (default gateway) is wrong — clients receive the incorrect gateway IP and cannot route off-subnet
DNS option 6 is not configured
The DHCP server lease time is too short
encounters.explanation: DHCP option 3 is the default gateway distributed to clients. If misconfigured (points to non-existent 192.168.1.1 instead of actual gateway 192.168.1.254), clients try to send off-subnet traffic to 192.168.1.1 — which doesn't exist or isn't a router. Fix: correct option 3 in the DHCP scope.

encounters.question: A server has a static IP 192.168.1.50 configured. The DHCP scope also includes 192.168.1.50 in its range. After adding a new workstation, connectivity issues occur. What is happening?
options: The DHCP scope is exhausted
The DHCP server assigns 192.168.1.50 to the new workstation — duplicate IP with the server causes ARP conflicts
The new workstation's NIC is faulty
The default VLAN is misconfigured
encounters.explanation: Static IPs within a DHCP range cause IP conflicts — the DHCP server doesn't know about the static assignment and may lease the same IP. Fix: (1) exclude all static IPs from the DHCP scope using DHCP exclusion ranges, or (2) use DHCP reservations (bind IP to MAC). Always exclude static IPs from DHCP pools.

encounters.question: After moving a server to a new subnet, internal users cannot reach it by name even though they can ping the server's new IP directly. What is most likely the problem?
options: The server's NIC failed during the move
The DNS A record for the server still points to the old IP — update the DNS record to the new IP
The server's default gateway needs updating
The DHCP lease for the server has expired
encounters.explanation: Ping by IP works = Layer 3 routing correct. Name fails = DNS stale record. The DNS server still has the old IP for the server's hostname. Fix: update the DNS A record to the new IP, then flush DNS cache on clients (ipconfig /flushdns) if the old record is still cached.

encounters.question: ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew fails to get a new IP address. The user gets 169.254.x.x. What should you investigate?
options: Whether the user typed the commands correctly
DHCP server availability — is it running? Can the client reach it? Is the scope exhausted?
Whether TLS 1.3 is enabled
Whether 802.1X is configured on the switch port
encounters.explanation: APIPA after manual release/renew = the DHCP DISCOVER broadcast from the client got no response. Investigate: (1) Is the DHCP server running? (2) Is there a DHCP relay if the server is on a different subnet? (3) Is the scope exhausted? (4) Is the switch port in the correct VLAN?

encounters.question: Certificate errors start appearing on all domain-joined Windows computers exactly 12 hours after an NTP server went offline. Why?
options: NTP outage caused the firewall rules to expire
Clock skew exceeded 5 minutes — Kerberos authentication is failing, causing certificate validation to fail as domain auth is required
The CA certificate expired simultaneously
DNS stopped resolving the certificate server
encounters.explanation: Without NTP, Windows clocks drift. After sufficient drift (>5 minutes from domain time), Kerberos authentication fails — domain computers cannot authenticate to domain controllers. Many certificate operations (OCSP, CRL, TLS auth) depend on successful domain authentication. Fixing NTP and resyncing time resolves the cascade.

guardian_encounters.question: What is Step 1 of CompTIA's troubleshooting methodology?
options: Implement the solution
Document findings
Identify the problem
Test the theory
guardian_encounters.explanation: Step 1: Identify the problem — gather info, identify symptoms, reproduce the issue, ask what changed. Never skip this: understanding the problem before theorising prevents wasted effort.

guardian_encounters.question: A host shows IP 169.254.12.5. What does this mean and what should you check first?
options: Valid static IP — check routing table
APIPA — DHCP failed. Check DHCP server status and scope availability.
IPv6 link-local — check IPv6 config
Subnet is exhausted — check all addresses
guardian_encounters.explanation: 169.254.x.x = APIPA. The host connected to the network but received no DHCP response. Check: DHCP server running? Scope has addresses? Relay configured if server is on another subnet? Switch VLAN correct?

guardian_encounters.question: An OTDR is the correct tool for which task?
options: Testing copper patch cable continuity
Locating a break in a fiber optic cable and measuring distance to the fault
Tracing an unlabelled cable through a wall
Scanning for open ports on a server
guardian_encounters.explanation: OTDR sends a light pulse into fiber, measures backscattered reflections, and reports: exact distance to breaks, splice quality, connector loss, and total end-to-end loss. Essential for fiber troubleshooting.

guardian_encounters.question: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse websites. nslookup returns NXDOMAIN for all queries. What is the problem?
options: Default gateway is wrong
DNS — the hostname being looked up doesn't exist in DNS (or wrong DNS server configured)
IP routing is broken
TLS certificate error
guardian_encounters.explanation: Ping 8.8.8.8 works = IP routing fine. NXDOMAIN from nslookup = DNS can reach the server but no record exists for that name, OR the wrong DNS server is queried. Check: ipconfig /all to see DNS server, verify it's correct, check the DNS record exists.

guardian_encounters.question: Traceroute shows * * * at hop 5 but hop 6 responds normally. What does this mean?
options: Hop 5 is down — traffic is being rerouted around it
Hop 5 does not respond to ICMP TTL-exceeded messages — traffic is still flowing through it
Hop 5 has packet loss
There is a routing loop at hop 5
guardian_encounters.explanation: * * * = no ICMP TTL-exceeded response received — the router likely rate-limits or drops these messages. Since hop 6 responds, traffic IS passing through hop 5 — it's not down. This is normal for many ISP routers.

guardian_encounters.question: After implementing a fix, what MUST you do before documenting?
options: Escalate to confirm the fix is approved
Verify full system functionality AND check for side effects from the change
Restart all affected services
Notify the CAB of the change
guardian_encounters.explanation: Step 6: Verify full system functionality. Confirm the original problem is resolved AND that the fix didn't break anything else. Only after successful verification should you proceed to Step 7 (documentation).

guardian_encounters.question: T568A and T568B differ because:
options: They use different cable categories (Cat5e vs Cat6)
The orange and green wire pairs are swapped between the two standards
T568A uses 4 pairs; T568B uses 2 pairs
They specify different maximum cable lengths
guardian_encounters.explanation: T568A and T568B only differ in that orange (pins 1,2) and green (pins 3,6) pairs are swapped. Both are valid EIA/TIA standards. A cable with T568A on one end and T568B on the other = crossover cable.

guardian_encounters.question: NTP failure causes Kerberos authentication to fail. Why?
options: NTP is required for DHCP leases to remain valid
Kerberos requires all domain clocks to be within 5 minutes of each other — time skew beyond that causes authentication rejection
NTP provides the encryption keys for Kerberos tickets
NTP failure causes DNS records to expire
guardian_encounters.explanation: Kerberos tickets include timestamps and have a 5-minute clock skew tolerance (configurable but default is 5 min). If a client's clock drifts more than 5 minutes from the KDC (domain controller), ticket validation fails — authentication rejected. NTP keeps all clocks synchronised. NTP uses UDP 123.

guardian_encounters.question: A cable passes continuity testing but has high errors at Gigabit speed. The most likely cause is:
options: Cable too long for Cat6
Split pair — wires from different pairs twisted together cause crosstalk that passes continuity but fails at high speeds
Open circuit on pair 4
Wrong connector type (RJ45 vs RJ11)
guardian_encounters.explanation: Split pairs pass a basic continuity test (all 8 pins connected) but fail performance tests. Untwisted wires from mismatched pairs create high NEXT (Near-End CrossTalk) that corrupts Gigabit signals. Only a proper wire map tester with pair identification catches this.

guardian_encounters.question: Two hosts on the same subnet have the same static IP. What symptom will be observed?
options: The switch disables both ports
Intermittent connectivity for both hosts — ARP replies from both confuse other devices about which MAC owns that IP
One host takes priority and the other is completely blocked
Both hosts share the same MAC address
guardian_encounters.explanation: Duplicate IP → ARP conflict: both machines respond to ARP requests for the same IP. Other hosts' ARP caches flip between both MACs. Traffic intended for the IP gets delivered to whichever machine won the last ARP race — intermittent for both. OS-level ARP conflict warnings may appear.

guardian_encounters.question: Which Windows command clears the local DNS resolver cache?
options: arp -d
netstat -f
ipconfig /flushdns
route delete
guardian_encounters.explanation: ipconfig /flushdns clears the Windows DNS resolver cache — forces the host to re-query DNS for all future hostname lookups. Use when: DNS records have been updated but the host still resolves the old IP; stale cache entries causing wrong connections.

guardian_encounters.question: A Cisco switch port shows 'FastEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is down'. What does this indicate?
options: Physical cable is disconnected
Physical signal detected (Layer 1 up) but Layer 2 protocol not establishing — likely duplex mismatch, encapsulation mismatch, or remote end issue
The port is in spanning tree blocking state
VLAN is not configured on the port
guardian_encounters.explanation: 'Line up' = carrier detected on the wire (Layer 1 working). 'Protocol down' = Layer 2 keepalives failing. Common causes: duplex mismatch (FD vs HD), encapsulation mismatch on WAN links, remote device with 'shutdown' command, or keepalive timer mismatch.

guardian_encounters.question: Wi-Fi disconnects whenever a microwave is used nearby. The permanent fix is:
options: Reboot the AP when it happens
Replace the microwave
Move the client to a 5 GHz SSID — 5 GHz is not affected by 2.4 GHz microwave interference
Set the AP channel to 14
guardian_encounters.explanation: 5 GHz (802.11ac/n) is completely outside the microwave oven's 2.4 GHz interference band. Moving clients to 5 GHz permanently solves this. Channel 14 is illegal in most countries and doesn't solve the interference.

guardian_encounters.question: A user can reach local hosts but nothing beyond the gateway. show ip route on the gateway router shows no default route. What is the fix?
options: Add a DNS server entry
Add a default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to the ISP router
Enable NAT on the router
Expand the DHCP scope
guardian_encounters.explanation: Without a default route (0.0.0.0/0), the router drops all packets destined for unknown networks. 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 [ISP-gateway-IP]' adds the default route — all non-local traffic is forwarded to the ISP for internet routing.

guardian_encounters.question: DHCP scope exhaustion occurs when:
options: The DHCP server's disk is full
All IP addresses in the DHCP pool are currently leased — no IPs available for new devices
The DHCP relay agent is unreachable
The default gateway IP is wrong
guardian_encounters.explanation: DHCP scope exhaustion: every address in the configured range is assigned to a current or stale lease. New devices send DHCPDISCOVER but receive no DHCPOFFER. Fix: expand the scope, reduce lease duration, remove stale leases, or add address exclusions for static devices.

guardian_encounters.question: netstat -an on a server shows port 443 NOT in the LISTENING state. Users cannot reach the HTTPS website hosted on this server. What does this tell you?
options: The firewall is blocking port 443 inbound
The web server process is not running — it has not bound to port 443
The SSL certificate is expired
The DNS record points to the wrong IP
guardian_encounters.explanation: If port 443 is not in LISTENING state, the web server software is not running or failed to bind to the port. The service must be started first. A firewall block would show the port listening on the server but not reachable from outside — very different from no listener at all.

guardian_encounters.question: The toner probe (fox and hound) is used to:
options: Measure optical signal loss in fiber
Inject an audio tone and trace an unlabelled cable through walls and bundles
Test a switch port's send/receive hardware
Certify Cat6A cable to 10GbE standards
guardian_encounters.explanation: Fox and hound: tone generator at one end injects an audible signal; the probe detects it at the other end. Used to identify and trace unlabelled cables through walls, ceilings, conduits, and patch panel bundles without disrupting service.

guardian_encounters.question: A user has a static IP configured but it's within the DHCP range. Another device gets assigned the same IP. What is the correct fix?
options: Delete the static IP from the workstation
Exclude the static IP from the DHCP scope using a DHCP exclusion range
Change the DHCP scope to a different subnet
Enable DHCP snooping on the switch
guardian_encounters.explanation: The DHCP server is unaware of manual static assignments. Configure a DHCP exclusion range to exclude all static IPs from the DHCP pool — the server will never assign those addresses dynamically. Best practice: reserve a block (e.g., .1–.20) for static assignments and start DHCP scope at .21.

guardian_encounters.question: In the bottom-up OSI troubleshooting approach, you confirm Layer 1 (cable connected, link lights on) and Layer 2 (switch shows port up, MAC learned). Ping to gateway fails. Which layer is suspect?
options: Layer 1 — check cable again
Layer 2 — check MAC table
Layer 3 — check IP address, subnet mask, default gateway configuration
Layer 7 — check application firewall
guardian_encounters.explanation: Layer 1 and 2 confirmed OK. Ping to gateway fails = Layer 3 issue. Most likely: wrong IP address, wrong subnet mask (places gateway in different network), or wrong default gateway IP configured on the host. Run ipconfig /all and verify each value.

guardian_encounters.question: A LWAP stops working after a WLC failover. The backup WLC has a different IP. What must be configured for the APs to find the backup WLC?
options: Update the AP firmware manually
Configure DHCP option 43 with the backup WLC IP, or configure the AP with the backup WLC IP directly — APs need to know where to find the WLC
Add the AP SSID to the backup WLC manually
Reconfigure all 802.1X certificates
guardian_encounters.explanation: LWAPs discover the WLC via: DHCP option 43 (WLC IP), DNS lookup (CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER), or direct configuration. After WLC failover to a different IP, APs need to find the new WLC. Configure DHCP option 43 to list the backup WLC IP, or use WLC HA to maintain the same management IP.
